findings.title: The "numpy" backend would run Numba kernels, because JIT is the default
findings.description:
The design says NumPy is "the only backend that exists today". It describes the runner as "today's `engine.tick.tick`" (line 60) with the existing `BulkForce` instances (lines 138-141, 398-400).
- `src/migratory/engine/_jit_config.py:14` sets `USE_JIT_KERNELS = True` by default.
- Every force wrapper dispatches on it at call time: `flocking.py:82,192,326` and `herding.py:32,175`.
- So a "numpy" run through the existing forces would time Numba kernels and label them NumPy.
- The design never has the numpy backend set the flag to `False`.
- It also never says how `--all-backends` (line 481) would run a numpy backend and a numba backend in one process. The flag is a module global, so the backends would have to flip it between runs and restore it.
- Line 342 says slice 144 registers `numba` "via the engine's existing JIT-config flag". That admits the flag is the switch, but the design neither gives it to the numpy runner nor states that Numba already exists.
- The architecture's 3.14 ms `force_total` figure (arch line 55) is described as "NumPy vectorized". It is not comparable to a default-flag run today.

The design needs to:
- Pin the numpy backend to `USE_JIT_KERNELS=False`, with save and restore.
- Say how the flag is isolated between backends.
- Correct the "only backend that exists" claim.

findings.title: The workload schema uses 3D coordinates, but the engine is 2D
findings.description:
The `mid-flock.yaml` example gives `world_size: [200.0, 200.0, 200.0]` and 3-component `cluster_centers`.
- `src/migratory/__init__.py:4` sets `DIMS = 2`.
- `AgentState` arrays are `N×DIMS` (`state.py:52-54`).
- `tools/run_deterministic_trajectory.py:41` draws positions as `(n, 2)`.
- `KDTreeQuery.build` documents shape `(n, 2)`.
- A formation initializer following the documented schema would fail on shape, or silently mis-size.
- The scaffold in `workload.py:187-191` already rejects non-2-entry `world_size`, so it contradicts the design's own example YAML.
- The density figures (200³ volume) and the cluster radius of 30 are also wrong for a 2D world. The "mid-density" characterization has no basis.

findings.title: The design names force singletons that do not exist
findings.description:
The design says force names "resolve to module-level singleton instances … (e.g. `flocking.cohesion_force`)".
- No such symbol exists. The engine exposes classes (`CohesionForce`, `SeparationForce`, and so on) that the tools instantiate directly.
- The scaffold's `workload.py:67-74` builds its own registry, which the design never specifies.
- The registry also includes `propulsion`, which is not among the "five existing BulkForce implementations" at lines 138-141. The slice plan (arch line 34) lists six.
- Because forces are stateless, the shared instances are probably harmless. But a shared registry mutated across backends is an undeclared hidden dependency.

findings.title: The profile registry source is claimed but not verified
findings.description:
The design says `flocker` and `leader` map to "the existing `BehavioralProfile` constructors used in `config/default.yaml`". The only profile content I found there is a commented-out example (`config/default.yaml:145-162`). Nothing there is named `leader`.
- "The harness does not invent new profiles" is therefore false as written.
- The scaffold hard-codes new parameter sets, including a derived "leader".
- Both profiles use `max_neighbors=32`, so every workload takes the `all_capped` `query_knn_batch` fast path in `tick()` (`tick.py:74-85`). The general radius-query path is never benchmarked, and the design doesn't say so.

findings.title: Phase boundaries are undefined, and the two overhead statements contradict each other
findings.description:
The design says the five phases "correspond exactly to bracketed regions of the existing `tick()` body". They don't.
- `tick()` has no `csr_assembly` region. It has profile-array building (`tick.py:58-72`), the query, `exclude_self`, optional `apply_neighbor_cap`, and the `concatenate`/`cumsum` offset build (`tick.py:103-106`). The architecture calls this phase `self_excl_cap`.
- The design never says which phase gets the profile-array build, `exclude_self`, `apply_neighbor_cap`, `eval_indices` construction, `max_speeds` indexing, or `record_density`.
- Lines 287-290 say profile-attribute fancy indexing is "overhead" (total minus the five phases).
- Lines 697-699 say `all_radii = np.array(...)` is included in `force_total`. In `tick()` it runs before the query and is not in the force loop. One of the two statements is wrong, and the per-phase numbers depend on which.
- The 5-phase comparison against the architecture's reference budget (verification step 9) is meaningless without these assignments.

findings.title: `tick_instrumented` duplicates the whole tick, and a bit-equality test cannot catch boundary drift
findings.description:
- The design calls the duplication "small (~5 lines per phase)". It is a copy of about 90 lines of `tick()` logic: both the fast path and the general path, the cap, CSR build, force loop, integrate, and density record.
- It is the only reason `bench/` carries engine logic.
- The drift mitigation (bit-equality test) catches algorithm drift but not phase-boundary drift. The design admits this, and the phase breakdown is the harness's entire reason to exist.
- Option (A) is dismissed as "bloat" and as forcing every backend to expose hooks. A keyword-only, default-`None` timer parameter on `tick()` would be one `if` per boundary, and it still wouldn't oblige other backends to expose hooks. Alternatively, `tick()` could be split into phase functions that both paths call.
- At minimum, the design should justify why a fork of the tick was chosen over a single shared code path.

findings.title: The harness cannot be added to by a single file, because backend registration depends on an import
findings.description:
`register_backend` is a decorator in `backends/__init__.py`. A backend module registers itself only when it is imported.
- The design specifies no import or discovery mechanism, so `get_backend("numpy")` would hit `KeyError` unless something imports `numpy_backend`.
- If `__init__.py` imports it, the result is a circular import (`numpy_backend` imports `register_backend` from `__init__`).
- If `__init__.py` imports each backend, adding a backend is not "one file and zero changes elsewhere" (lines 586-591).
- Either specify auto-discovery (for example `pkgutil`) or explicit import lines, and correct the integration requirement.
- `--list-backends` (verification step 1) depends on the same unresolved choice.

findings.title: Per-force timing is deferred, though the slice plan assigns it to 141
findings.description:
The slice plan entry (plan line 26) requires timings "broken down by phase (… force totals per force, integration)". The design ships one `force_total` and pushes per-force timing to slice 142.
- Slice 142's plan entry never says it extends the harness.
- Doing so would change `PhaseTimings`, bump `schema_version`, and edit the harness. That contradicts the "one file, no harness changes" promise (lines 525-526, 586-591).
- Slice 142 benchmarks a single force (Cohesion) against Numba and NumPy, so it needs exactly this resolution.
- The cost is a `perf_counter_ns` pair around each force in the loop. It is trivial now and costly to retrofit.
- Pre-plan `PhaseTimings` is already shaped for the change, so deferring it saves nothing.

findings.title: Other scope the plan assigns to 141 is dropped silently
findings.description:
- The plan says reports include "the formation-dependent breakdown noted in the architecture's Profile Principle". The design has three workloads and a per-workload table. Nothing produces a cross-formation comparison.
- The plan names "CSV/JSON" output. The design drops CSV without comment. That is probably fine, but say so.
- The Numba backend is deferred to "slice 144 / 118" (lines 92, 341, 589). The slice plan says 142 benchmarks Quadrants "against the existing NumPy and Numba implementations" and depends on (118) and (141). 142 therefore needs a Numba runner before 144.
- Numba already exists (finding 1), so a numba runner is a small addition that belongs in this slice, or the design should state that 142 adds it.
- Slice 144's plan entry does not list a Numba runner either.

findings.title: The parity hash cannot serve the downstream use the design claims
findings.description:
- Line 473 says a downstream consumer will "interpret [the hash] within the documented tolerance band". A SHA-256 over raw bytes cannot be compared within a tolerance. One ULP difference changes the whole digest.
- The slice plan (plan lines 36, 78) needs tolerance-based tick-level parity for GPU reductions.
- Line 534 says slice 145's parity test "consumes the harness's NumPy parity hash as the reference". That would give a bit-exact check where 145 needs a tolerance check.
- The harness should keep the post-run positions and velocities, or a sample or summary of them, alongside the hash. Otherwise 145 has to rebuild the reference itself.
- The spec is also inconsistent about when the hash is taken. Line 81 says "post-warmup". Line 460 says "after the measure phase".
- `AgentState` is mutated in place and the `TickResult` is a view. The design must say whether the hash is taken before `finalize()`.

findings.title: The spatial backend benchmarked is not the "default operating point"
findings.description:
- The design says `mid-flock` is the "current default operating point", "roughly equivalent to the live-server default config", but hard-codes `KDTreeQuery`. `config/default.yaml:126-129` documents the default as the adaptive backend.
- `KDTreeQuery` is described in `kd_tree.py:1-7` as opt-in.
- Line 542 gives the path as `engine.spatial.KDTreeQuery`. The class lives in `migratory.spatial.kd_tree`.
- The architecture's budget figures are explicitly "KD-tree backend, N=2492" (arch line 50). The N=3500 mid-flock is then compared against an N≈2500 table (step 9), which is not like for like.
- Spatial backend choice should be a workload or backend parameter. Slice 143 needs it to compare `KDTreeQuery` against `QuadrantsSpatialQuery`.

findings.title: Workload parameters are not fully specified
findings.description:
- Scope line 70 promises fields for "density" and "formation seed". The schema has neither. It has `n`, `seed`, and a formation block.
- No parameters are given for `dispersed` or `packed-herd`: not N, not world size or cluster radius, not a density target. The three-regime claim can't be checked.
- It's also unspecified how initial velocities are generated, and whether `seed` drives positions only or also profile assignment and velocities.
- That matters because the parity hash is taken "for a fixed seed".
- Profile fractions are not validated to sum to 1 or to produce integer counts. The `uniform` and `packed` kinds are unspecified.
- Slice 143 expects N up to 250k and "a `large-N` workload at N=50k" (line 528). The NumPy path at that size is untested, and no workload size limit is stated.

findings.title: CLI and operator walkthrough have gaps
findings.description:
- The CLI section lists `--workload`, `--backend`, `--all-backends`, and `--workload-dir`. The walkthrough uses `--list-backends` and `--list-workloads`, which are never specified.
- `--workload mid-flock` resolution is unspecified. The workloads live at repo root while the package lives under `src/`. It is not stated whether lookup is relative to the cwd, or to the repo root found via `__file__`.
- Nothing says `bench/results/` is created. The `.gitkeep` and `.gitignore` entries already exist in the tree, but the design neither relies on them nor says the writer calls `mkdir`.
- The "UTC ISO timestamp" in the filename (line 236) contains colons unless a format is fixed.
- Result files from several runs accumulate. The Markdown renderer says "one row per backend across all backends in `bench/results/`" (line 440). Which run is selected per backend is not stated. Walkthrough step 6 (three tables on stdout) implies a different behavior from step 3 (one numpy row).
- The "sortable on TPS" claim is meaningless for a static Markdown table.
- `git rev-parse HEAD` is shown as a short SHA in the sample (`fc989bf`). If the run happens outside a git checkout or on a dirty tree, the failure behavior and dirty-flag recording are undefined.

findings.title: Failure modes miss the runtime paths that matter
findings.description:
- Only `setup` raising is covered. `tick_once` raising mid-measure is not. Does the run still write a partial report, or nothing? Is `finalize` still called?
- Result writing is not atomic. A run killed during the write leaves a truncated JSON in `bench/results/`. The Markdown renderer reads every file in that directory, so one bad file would break all later reports. Nothing says the renderer skips or rejects such a file.
- Old-reader rejection of unknown `schema_version` (line 532) is stated but not wired to the renderer.
- A TPS below 1 is "warned and written", but there is no wall-clock bound. A 600-tick measure at under 1 TPS is a 10-minute stall. A GPU hang in a future backend has no timeout.
- A NaN or inf state mid-run (unstable force parameters at high density in `packed-herd`) is not detected. The hash and timings would be recorded for a diverged simulation.

findings.title: Timer accounting and statistics details are thin
findings.description:
- The per-tick `PhaseTimings` are collected inside the measured loop. The design does not say whether the list append, GC, or `perf_counter_ns` calls themselves are excluded.
- It does not address GC pauses or P99 over 600 samples. P99 of 600 samples is the 6th-worst value, and the design offers no confidence guidance.
- JSON sample values are formatted as floats but typed as ints in `PhaseTimings`. The aggregation returns floats (`runner.py:53`). The schema's number type is unspecified.
- `tps_observed` and `wall_seconds` are not defined. Is wall time the sum of tick times, or the loop's wall clock including timer overhead?

findings.title: The design restates other documents and leans on unneeded tooling
findings.description:
- The Value section and the three Open Questions mostly restate the architecture and slice plan. Each Open Question already carries its own "defer" recommendation. They can collapse to one line.
- Line 122-124 says the stub-backend tests "reuse" `pytest-benchmark`. Unit tests of timer arithmetic against a synthetic backend do not need it (and no existing benchmark test is present under `tests/`). Drop the claim, along with the "stays consistent" rationale.
- Walkthrough steps 7, 8, and 10 are checks of non-goals and `head -15` output. They don't verify slice behavior.
- A `--workload-dir` mode, and the `--all-backends` mode with a single backend, are unused for this slice's single backend.
- The "5 lines per phase" estimate and the "eight new files" effort figure (line 741) understate the real size. The component listing at lines 157-172 alone is 11 files, and 8 of the 12 steps are scaffolding.

findings.title: The design describes a package the worktree already partly contains
findings.description:
`src/migratory/bench/` already has `runner.py`, `workload.py`, `cli.py`, `__main__.py`, an empty `backends/__init__.py`, and `reports/__init__.py`.
- The design says "New package", with `status: not_started`.
- The scaffold diverges from the design in several places: 2D `world_size`, the `propulsion` force, `Workload` fields, and `aggregate()` semantics (population stdev).
- The scaffold comments reference task IDs (T1, T7, T19, T21), but the design has no task numbering.
- Reconcile the design with the code, or mark the scaffold as superseded.

findings.title: Stated counts could not be verified
findings.description:
"433 pre-existing pyright errors" and "1100 passed, 2 skipped" are stated as pass/fail pins.
- I did not run the suite or pyright.
- Pins like these go stale. "No new errors in `bench/`" and "existing suite passes unchanged" would be sturdier criteria.

findings.title: Dependency direction and boundary choices are sound
findings.description:
- The harness depends on the engine and spatial layers through `TickResult` and the existing APIs. Nothing in the engine or server depends on the harness.
- Keeping the world server, websockets, and `logging_sim` out of the benchmark is consistent with the architecture's "wire is separable" principle (arch line 46).
- Placing workload inputs outside `src/` is reasonable.
- `bench/results/*.json` and `*.md` are already gitignored (`.gitignore:173-174`).
- `pyyaml` is a declared dependency (`pyproject.toml:14`).
- `pytest-benchmark` is in the dev dependency group (`pyproject.toml:73`).
